options.text: It gets both sets, combined
options.rationale: Permissions aren't merged on a move.

questions.explanation: Child files inherit the parent's permissions by default. A copy takes the destination's permissions; a move within the same volume keeps its permissions; a move to another volume takes the destination's.
questions.discriminator_tested: Move within a volume keeps permissions; copy takes the destination's.

questions.stem: An admin renamed a sensitive share to 'Payroll$' so it no longer appears when users browse the server. Which answer about the data's protection is BEST?

options.text: It's secure; $ shares require administrator rights
options.rationale: The $ doesn't change who has access.

options.text: It's secure; SMB encrypts shares ending in $
options.rationale: A $ suffix has no effect on encryption.

options.text: Users can still type the path directly
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say what does protect the data: permissions.

options.text: The $ hides it from browsing but doesn't secure it
options.rationale: Correct: permissions still decide who gets in.

questions.explanation: Shared files and folders are published over SMB (TCP 445); hidden and administrative shares end in $ (C$, ADMIN$). The $ only hides a share from browsing; it does not secure it.
questions.discriminator_tested: $ only hides a share; it doesn't secure it.

questions.stem: Two users try to install software. One sees a Yes/No prompt; the other is asked for an administrator's password. What BEST explains the difference?

options.text: The first is an admin; the second is a standard user
options.rationale: Correct: consent prompt for admins, credential prompt for standard users.

options.text: The second machine has a stricter firewall profile
options.rationale: Firewall profiles don't produce UAC prompts.

options.text: The first is a standard user; the second is an admin
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: UAC is enabled on both machines
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't explain why the prompts differ.

questions.explanation: UAC prompts before actions that need administrative rights. Admins run with a standard token until they elevate: an admin sees a consent prompt, a standard user sees a credential prompt. It stops malware from silently gaining admin rights.
questions.discriminator_tested: Admin sees consent prompt; standard user sees credential prompt.

questions.stem: A Windows admin sees two pending updates: a monthly cumulative update released on the second Tuesday, and a new annual version of the OS. Which pair of labels fits them?

options.text: An application patch and a firmware update
options.rationale: Both are Windows OS updates.

options.text: Two security updates of different sizes
options.rationale: A new OS version is a feature update.

options.text: A feature update and a driver update
options.rationale: The monthly update is a security/quality update.

options.text: Security/quality and feature
options.rationale: Correct: Patch Tuesday cumulative update, then a new OS version.

questions.explanation: Windows Update delivers OS security, quality, and feature updates; WSUS or Intune can centralize control. Monthly cumulative security updates arrive on Patch Tuesday (the second Tuesday); feature updates deliver a new OS version.
questions.discriminator_tested: Monthly cumulative security updates vs feature updates.

questions.stem: Each PC shows 'Windows is up to date', yet a scan finds a critical flaw in the installed PDF reader. What BEST explains this?

options.text: OS updates don't cover most third-party apps
options.rationale: Correct: the PDF reader needs its own update process.

options.text: The PDF reader needs its own update
options.rationale: That is the fix, not the explanation.

options.text: The flaw is in the PC's firmware
options.rationale: It is in an application.

options.text: The scanner may be out of date
options.rationale: The flaw is real; Windows Update simply doesn't cover it.

questions.explanation: Application patching: third-party applications need their own update process. Patching the OS doesn't patch most third-party apps, such as browsers, PDF readers, and runtimes.
questions.discriminator_tested: Patching the OS doesn't patch most third-party apps.

questions.stem: A new network card works only after the technician installs software from the card's vendor that runs in the Windows kernel. What did the vendor supply?

options.text: A device driver
options.rationale: Correct: OS-side software that talks to the hardware.

options.text: Firmware for the card
options.rationale: Firmware runs on the card itself, not in Windows.

options.text: An application patch
options.rationale: Applications run in user mode, not the kernel.

options.text: A UEFI update
options.rationale: UEFI is the PC's boot firmware.

questions.explanation: A device driver is software that lets the OS communicate with hardware, and it runs in kernel mode. Firmware is code on the device itself. 64-bit Windows requires signed kernel drivers.
questions.discriminator_tested: Driver = OS-side software; firmware = code on the device.

questions.stem: A Mac user downloads an app from a developer's website, and macOS checks that the developer is identified and the app is notarized before it will open. Which feature performed the check?

options.text: Gatekeeper
options.rationale: Correct: it controls apps from outside the store.

options.text: The Mac App Store
options.rationale: The app didn't come from the store.

options.text: The application firewall
options.rationale: The firewall controls network connections, not launches.

options.text: Software Update
options.rationale: Software Update installs macOS updates.

questions.explanation: The Mac App Store is Apple-reviewed, sandboxed app distribution. Gatekeeper controls apps from outside the store, allowing identified or notarized developers; the App Store is the curated source.
questions.discriminator_tested: Gatekeeper controls apps from outside the App Store.

questions.stem: An admin runs the command below on an Ubuntu server. What BEST describes what it updates?
questions.exhibit:
$ sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
The following packages will be upgraded:
  openssl  linux-image-6.8.0-45  firefox  libreoffice-core  nginx
5 upgraded, 0 newly installed, 0 to remove and 0 not upgraded.

options.text: OS and repo apps together
options.rationale: Correct: kernel, libraries, and applications from the repositories.

options.text: The kernel alone; apps update themselves
options.rationale: Firefox, LibreOffice, and nginx are in the list.

options.text: The server's firmware and drivers
options.rationale: apt updates software packages, not device firmware.

options.text: Security packages for the server
options.rationale: Some are, but apt updates applications too.

questions.explanation: System updates on macOS come from Apple's Software Update; on Linux, package managers such as apt (Debian/Ubuntu) and dnf/yum (Red Hat/Fedora) update the OS and repo-installed apps together.
questions.discriminator_tested: A Linux package manager updates the OS and repo apps together.

questions.stem: Which sequence BEST reflects a patch management process?

options.text: Identify, deploy, test, approve, inventory, document, verify
options.rationale: Deploying before testing skips the safety check.

options.text: Inventory, deploy, identify, test, approve, verify, document
options.rationale: You can't deploy before identifying what is needed.

options.text: Deploy, verify, document, inventory, identify, test, approve
options.rationale: Deploying first defeats the purpose of the process.

options.text: Inventory, identify, test, approve, deploy, verify, document
options.rationale: Correct: know what you have, then test before deploying.

questions.explanation: Patch management is an ongoing process: inventory, identify, evaluate and test, approve, deploy, verify, and document. It is a managed process, not a single update: test before production and keep a rollback plan.
questions.discriminator_tested: A managed process: test before production.

questions.stem: An admin at 10.1.4.20 can't SSH to a Linux host whose firewall shows the status below. What BEST explains it?
questions.exhibit:
$ sudo ufw status verbose
Status: active
Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing)
To          Action     From
22/tcp      ALLOW IN   10.1.9.0/24
443/tcp     ALLOW IN   Anywhere

options.text: Incoming traffic is denied by default
options.rationale: True, but it misses that SSH is allowed from one subnet.

options.text: ufw blocks SSH whenever HTTPS is open
options.rationale: Rules are independent.

options.text: Rules are per application, as on macOS
options.rationale: Linux rules are port- and address-based.

options.text: SSH is allowed from 10.1.9.0/24 alone
options.rationale: Correct: 10.1.4.20 isn't in that range, so the default deny applies.

questions.explanation: On Linux, netfilter is managed with iptables/nftables or front-ends such as ufw and firewalld, using port- and address-based rules. The macOS application firewall is off by default and sets rules per application.
questions.discriminator_tested: Linux firewall rules are port/address-based; ufw is a front-end.

questions.stem: User dave belongs to the finance group and tries to run the script below. What happens?

options.text: It runs; the group has read and execute
options.rationale: Correct: r-x for the group.

options.text: It fails; the owner alone can run it
options.rationale: The group also has execute.

options.text: It fails; others have no permissions
options.rationale: dave is in the group, so the 'others' bits don't apply.

options.text: It runs, and dave can also edit it
options.rationale: The group has no write permission.

questions.explanation: Linux permissions are read, write, and execute for owner, group, and others. rwxr-x--- (numeric 750) gives the owner full access, the group read and execute, and others nothing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Three sets = owner, group, others.

questions.stem: A technician is flashing new BIOS/UEFI firmware on a server when the power fails halfway through. What is the MOST likely result?

options.text: The update will need to be run again
options.rationale: Possibly, but only if the device can still boot to run it.

options.text: The OS will roll back to the previous driver
options.rationale: Driver rollback is an OS feature; this is firmware.

options.text: The server may not boot until the firmware is recovered
options.rationale: Correct: an interrupted firmware update can brick the device.

options.text: Nothing; firmware updates resume automatically
options.rationale: Most don't, which is why interruption is dangerous.

questions.explanation: Driver and firmware updates fix bugs and vulnerabilities in drivers and device firmware (BIOS/UEFI, NICs, storage). Get them from the vendor and verify their integrity; interrupting a firmware update can brick the device.
questions.discriminator_tested: Interrupting a firmware update can brick the device.

questions.stem: A lab instrument's controller PC runs an OS that has reached end of support, and the vendor won't certify a newer OS. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Re-enable automatic updates on it
options.rationale: No updates are coming.

options.text: Wait for the vendor's next OS patch
options.rationale: After end of support there are no more security patches.

options.text: Isolate it on its own segment
options.rationale: Correct: if it can't be patched or upgraded, limit its exposure.

options.text: Keep it, with antivirus kept up to date
options.rationale: Helps a little, but leaves unpatchable flaws exposed to the network.

questions.explanation: The OS life cycle runs from release through mainstream and extended support to end of support. After end of support there are no security patches, so unpatchable systems must be upgraded, replaced, or isolated.
questions.discriminator_tested: After end of support: upgrade, replace, or isolate.

questions.stem: An analyst opens the event below in Event Viewer. What BEST describes what it records?
questions.exhibit:
Log Name:      Security
Source:        Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing
Event ID:      4625
Keywords:      Audit Failure
Account Name:  administrator
Logon Type:    10
Source Network Address: 198.51.100.77

options.text: A security event for the administrator account
options.rationale: True, but vague; it doesn't say a logon failed.

options.text: A successful logon from 198.51.100.77
options.rationale: Success would be 4624 and Audit Success.

options.text: A failed remote admin logon
options.rationale: Correct: 4625 is a failed logon; type 10 is a remote (RDP) logon.

options.text: A driver failure logged by the system
options.rationale: Driver events go to the System log.

questions.explanation: Event Viewer's Security log records logons and audited actions (Audit Success/Failure), such as 4624 for a logon and 4625 for a failed logon. The System log covers OS components and drivers; Application covers programs.
questions.discriminator_tested: Security log: 4624 logon, 4625 failed logon.

questions.stem: What BEST describes the purpose of audit logs?

options.text: A backup of user files for recovery
options.rationale: Logs aren't backups.

options.text: A trail of who did what, when, and from where
options.rationale: Correct: an accountability trail.

options.text: A record of system errors for troubleshooting
options.rationale: That describes the System and Application logs.

options.text: A record of security events
options.rationale: True, but it misses the point: accountability for actions.

questions.explanation: Audit logs record security-relevant actions: who, what, when, and from where. Windows audit policy or Linux auditd enables them; they are an accountability trail and must be protected from tampering.
questions.discriminator_tested: Audit logs = accountability trail; protect from tampering.

questions.stem: Routers send syslog messages to a collector across the WAN on UDP 514. What is the BEST concern?

options.text: Syslog carries critical messages alone
options.rationale: Syslog carries every severity level.

options.text: Some messages may be dropped in transit
options.rationale: True, but it misses that they can also be read.

options.text: UDP 514 may be blocked by some firewalls
options.rationale: A configuration issue, not the inherent weakness.

options.text: It's cleartext and unreliable
options.rationale: Correct: readable in transit, and UDP can drop messages.

questions.explanation: Syslog is the standard protocol for sending log messages, by default over UDP 514, which is cleartext and unreliable. TCP or TLS (port 6514) adds reliability and security.
questions.discriminator_tested: UDP 514 is cleartext and unreliable; TLS 6514 adds security.

questions.stem: An attacker gains admin access to a router and erases its local log buffer. What BEST explains why the company still has a record of the intrusion?

options.text: The router also logs to its own memory
options.rationale: That buffer is what was erased.

options.text: Logs were stored somewhere other than the router
options.rationale: True, but vague about where and how.

options.text: The SIEM restores deleted router logs
options.rationale: A SIEM can analyze what it received but can't undelete anything.

options.text: Copies were already sent to a central syslog server
options.rationale: Correct: the centralized copy survives the device being wiped.

questions.explanation: A syslog collector is a central server receiving syslog from many devices. The centralized copy survives if a device is compromised or wiped; it needs consistent time (NTP).
questions.discriminator_tested: A central copy survives a compromised or wiped device.

questions.stem: What is the severity of the message below?
questions.exhibit: *Oct 21 10:42:13: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down

options.text: 1, Alert
options.rationale: The middle number is 3.

options.text: 3, Error
options.rationale: Correct: the number in the middle of the mnemonic.

options.text: 0, Emergency
options.rationale: Emergency is reserved for an unusable system.

options.text: 5, Notification
options.rationale: Link-protocol messages often use 5, but this one is 3.

questions.explanation: Cisco syslog messages follow the format sequence, timestamp, %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC: description. The number in the middle is the severity level, here 3, Error.
questions.discriminator_tested: The middle number is the severity.

questions.stem: A router is configured with 'logging trap 4'. Which messages does it send to the syslog server?

options.text: Level 4 alone, warnings
options.rationale: The level is a threshold, not a single level.

options.text: Levels 0 to 4: warnings and worse
options.rationale: Correct: level N sends N and everything more severe.

options.text: Levels 4 through 7, warnings and less severe
options.rationale: Lower numbers are more severe; this is reversed.

options.text: Each level except 4
options.rationale: No such setting.

questions.explanation: Logging levels run 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notification, 6 Informational, 7 Debugging. A lower number is more severe, and setting level N logs N and everything more severe (0 to N).
questions.discriminator_tested: Lower number = more severe; level N logs 0 to N.

questions.stem: A server's Security log shows the entries below. Which two are the STRONGEST signs of malicious activity? (Choose two.)
questions.exhibit:
02:13  4624  Logon success                    user=svc-backup  src=10.1.9.40
02:14  4720  User account created             new=helpdesk2    by=svc-backup
02:14  4732  Member added to Administrators   member=helpdesk2
02:20  1102  The audit log was cleared        by=helpdesk2
09:05  4624  Logon success                    user=jlee        src=10.1.4.22

options.text: The audit log being cleared at 02:20
options.rationale: Correct: clearing the Security log (1102) is itself a red flag.

options.text: The service account logging on at 02:13
options.rationale: A backup account logging on at night may be normal.

options.text: A new account added to Administrators at 02:14
options.rationale: Correct: a new admin account created by a service account at night.

options.text: jlee logging on at 09:05
options.rationale: A normal start-of-day logon.

options.text: The log using Event ID 4624 for logons
options.rationale: That is just the standard logon event.

questions.explanation: Identifying anomalies means comparing log activity to a baseline: off-hours logons, repeated failed logons, new admin accounts, unusual traffic. A cleared Security log (Event ID 1102) is itself a red flag.
questions.discriminator_tested: New admin accounts and a cleared log (1102) are red flags.

questions.stem: A company already sends its logs to a syslog collector. What is the MAIN thing a SIEM would add?

options.text: Longer log retention
options.rationale: A SIEM does retain logs, but storage isn't what sets it apart.

options.text: Encryption of syslog over UDP 514
options.rationale: That needs syslog over TLS, not a SIEM.

options.text: Collection of logs from devices
options.rationale: The collector already does that.

options.text: Cross-source correlation
options.rationale: Correct: it analyzes and links events across sources, with alerts.

questions.explanation: A SIEM aggregates, normalizes, and correlates logs from many sources, with alerts, dashboards, and retention. A syslog collector stores logs; a SIEM analyzes them.
questions.discriminator_tested: Collector stores logs; SIEM correlates and analyzes.

questions.stem: A laptop moves from the office domain network to a hotel's Wi-Fi. What BEST describes what changes in Windows Defender Firewall?

options.text: It uses the Public profile
options.rationale: Correct: the active profile follows the network location.

options.text: Outbound traffic becomes blocked by default
options.rationale: Outbound is allowed by default on every profile.

options.text: Inbound traffic is blocked unless allowed
options.rationale: True on every profile, so it isn't what changes.

options.text: It keeps the Domain profile's rules
options.rationale: The Domain profile applies only on the domain network.

questions.explanation: Windows Defender Firewall has separate Domain, Private, and Public profiles. Inbound is blocked unless a rule allows it, outbound is allowed by default, and the active profile depends on network location.
questions.discriminator_tested: The active profile depends on network location.

questions.stem: Which two are reasons attackers favour built-in scripting tools such as PowerShell? (Choose two.)

options.text: They require no user account to run
options.rationale: Scripts run under an account like anything else.

options.text: Windows has no way to log them
options.rationale: PowerShell logging exists; it just has to be enabled.

options.text: Execution policy blocks defenders from using them
options.rationale: Execution policy isn't a security boundary for anyone.

options.text: They are already installed and trusted
options.rationale: Correct: nothing new has to be brought onto the system.

options.text: Their activity blends in with normal admin work
options.rationale: Correct: 'living off the land' is harder to spot.

questions.explanation: Scripting automates admin tasks with PowerShell, batch, VBScript, or Python, the same tools attackers use ('living off the land'). PowerShell's execution policy is a safety setting, not a security boundary.
questions.discriminator_tested: Attackers use the same built-in tools: living off the land.

questions.stem: A new laptop image is being prepared. Which single change BEST limits the damage if a user opens malware?

options.text: Daily work under a standard, non-admin account
options.rationale: Correct: malware inherits the user's limited rights.

options.text: BitLocker encryption on the system drive
options.rationale: Protects data on a lost laptop, not against running malware.

options.text: Turning off Windows Update to avoid reboots
options.rationale: That increases risk.

options.text: A hidden C$ share for administrators
options.rationale: Hiding a share doesn't limit malware.

questions.explanation: Windows security considerations reduce attack surface with layered controls: daily use as a standard user, disabling unused accounts and services, antimalware, and disk encryption.
questions.discriminator_tested: Standard-user daily use limits damage.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes how NTFS permissions from a user's several groups combine?

options.text: Additive, but Deny overrides
options.rationale: Correct: cumulative, with Deny overriding Allow.

options.text: The group listed first in the ACL wins
options.rationale: Order of listing doesn't decide NTFS access.

options.text: The most restrictive group permission wins
options.rationale: That rule applies when combining share and NTFS permissions.

options.text: They add up across the user's groups
options.rationale: True, but it leaves out that Deny overrides Allow.

questions.explanation: NTFS permissions apply to both local and network access, are cumulative across groups, and Deny overrides Allow. Full control adds change permissions and take ownership over Modify.
questions.discriminator_tested: Cumulative across groups; Deny overrides Allow.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why share permissions have no effect on a user working at the file server's own keyboard?

options.text: Share permissions apply to network access alone
options.rationale: Correct: locally, only NTFS applies.

options.text: NTFS is disabled for local sessions
options.rationale: NTFS is exactly what applies locally.

options.text: The user isn't connecting through the share
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't state the rule behind it.

options.text: Local users are treated as administrators
options.rationale: Local users keep their normal rights.

questions.explanation: Local permissions cover a user logged on at the machine itself. Only NTFS permissions apply locally; share permissions are ignored.
questions.discriminator_tested: Only NTFS applies locally.

questions.stem: To simplify management, admins set every share's permission to Full Control for authenticated users and control access with NTFS. What BEST describes the effect for users connecting over the network?

options.text: NTFS permissions alone decide their access
options.rationale: Correct: the share no longer restricts, so the more restrictive layer is NTFS.

options.text: Local users lose their NTFS permissions
options.rationale: Share settings don't affect local access.

options.text: Network access is simpler to troubleshoot
options.rationale: A benefit, but not the effect on access.

options.text: Everyone gets Full Control over the network
options.rationale: NTFS still restricts; the most restrictive applies.

questions.explanation: Share permissions apply only to network access, and combined with NTFS the more restrictive is the effective access. With shares at Full Control, NTFS decides.
questions.discriminator_tested: Network: most restrictive of share and NTFS.

questions.stem: A file in D:\HR has an explicit permission granting HR Modify. It is copied to D:\Public, where Everyone has inherited Read. What permissions does the copy have?

options.text: Public's permissions; copies inherit
options.rationale: Correct: a copy is a new file that takes the destination's permissions.

options.text: Both sets combined
options.rationale: Permissions aren't merged.

options.text: No permissions until an admin sets them
options.rationale: New files always inherit from the destination.

options.text: HR: Modify, carried with the file
options.rationale: That happens on a move within the same volume, not a copy.

questions.explanation: Child files inherit the parent's permissions by default. A copy takes the destination's permissions; a move within the same volume keeps its permissions; a move to another volume takes the destination's.
questions.discriminator_tested: Copy takes the destination's permissions.

questions.stem: An auditor reviews the output below from a file server. Which statement is BEST?
questions.exhibit:
C:\> net share
Share name   Resource        Remark
C$           C:\             Default share
ADMIN$       C:\Windows      Remote Admin
IPC$                         Remote IPC
Projects     D:\Projects
Payroll$     D:\Payroll

options.text: C$ and ADMIN$ should be deleted at once
options.rationale: Administrative shares are defaults; the risk lies in their permissions.

options.text: Several folders are shared over SMB
options.rationale: True, but it misses the security point.

options.text: Payroll$ is encrypted because of the $
options.rationale: The $ has nothing to do with encryption.

options.text: Payroll$ is hidden, not secured
options.rationale: Correct: the $ keeps it out of browse lists only.

questions.explanation: Shared folders are published over SMB (TCP 445); hidden and administrative shares end in $ (C$, ADMIN$). The $ only hides a share from browsing; it does not secure it.
questions.discriminator_tested: $ only hides a share.

questions.stem: Which threat does UAC MOST directly reduce?

options.text: Attackers guessing account passwords
options.rationale: Lockout and strong passwords address that.

options.text: Network worms spreading over SMB
options.rationale: Patching and firewalls address that.

options.text: Malware silently gaining admin rights
options.rationale: Correct: elevation needs an explicit prompt.

options.text: Users running programs they downloaded
options.rationale: Programs that don't need admin rights run without a prompt.

questions.explanation: UAC prompts before actions that need administrative rights. Admins run with a standard token until they elevate, so malware can't silently gain admin rights.
questions.discriminator_tested: UAC stops malware from silently gaining admin.

questions.stem: A company with 800 PCs wants to approve, schedule, and report on Windows updates centrally. Which option BEST fits?

options.text: WSUS or Intune
options.rationale: Correct: centralized control of Windows Update.

options.text: Windows Update on each PC
options.rationale: Works, but gives no central approval or reporting.

options.text: The apt package manager
options.rationale: apt is for Debian and Ubuntu Linux.

options.text: Group Policy firewall rules
options.rationale: Firewall rules don't manage updates.

questions.explanation: Windows Update delivers OS security, quality, and feature updates; WSUS or Intune centralize control.
questions.discriminator_tested: WSUS/Intune centralize Windows Update control.

questions.stem: Which two measures BEST close the gap where third-party applications go unpatched? (Choose two.)

options.text: Running Windows Update nightly instead of monthly
options.rationale: Windows Update doesn't patch most third-party apps.

options.text: An inventory of installed applications
options.rationale: Correct: you can't patch what you don't know is installed.

options.text: A tool that updates non-Microsoft software
options.rationale: Correct: apps need their own update process.

options.text: Removing users' local admin rights
options.rationale: Good hardening, but it doesn't patch anything.

options.text: Upgrading the PCs' firmware
options.rationale: Firmware isn't where application flaws live.

questions.explanation: Application patching: third-party applications need their own update process, because patching the OS doesn't patch most third-party apps such as browsers, PDF readers, and runtimes.
questions.discriminator_tested: Third-party apps need their own update process.

questions.stem: After a graphics driver update, a PC shows a blank screen at the login prompt. What is the BEST first step?

options.text: Reinstall Windows from scratch
options.rationale: Drastic when a rollback is available.

options.text: Flash the GPU's firmware
options.rationale: The change was to the driver, not the firmware.

options.text: Disable UAC so the driver can load
options.rationale: UAC isn't why the driver failed.

options.text: Boot to safe mode and roll back the driver
options.rationale: Correct: rollback restores the prior driver.

questions.explanation: A device driver lets the OS communicate with hardware and runs in kernel mode. Rollback restores the prior driver; firmware is separate code on the device itself.
questions.discriminator_tested: Rollback restores the prior driver.

questions.stem: Which source of macOS apps is reviewed by Apple and delivers sandboxed apps?

options.text: The Mac App Store
options.rationale: Correct: the curated source.

options.text: A notarized download
options.rationale: Notarization is an automated malware scan, not a review or sandbox.

options.text: A disk image from email
options.rationale: No review at all.

options.text: Homebrew packages
options.rationale: A third-party package manager.

questions.explanation: The Mac App Store is Apple-reviewed, sandboxed app distribution. Gatekeeper controls apps from outside the store.
questions.discriminator_tested: App Store = curated; Gatekeeper = outside the store.

questions.stem: Which command updates installed packages on a Red Hat Enterprise Linux server?

options.text: sudo dnf upgrade
options.rationale: Correct: dnf (or yum) on Red Hat systems.

options.text: softwareupdate -i -a
options.rationale: That is macOS.

options.text: wuauclt /detectnow
options.rationale: That is a legacy Windows Update client command.

options.text: sudo apt upgrade
options.rationale: apt is for Debian and Ubuntu.

questions.explanation: On Linux, package managers update the OS and repo apps together: apt on Debian/Ubuntu, and dnf/yum on Red Hat and Fedora. macOS updates come from Apple.
questions.discriminator_tested: apt on Debian/Ubuntu; dnf/yum on Red Hat/Fedora.

questions.stem: A team pushed a patch to its 300 servers on the day it was released, and a third of them crashed. Which patch management step was skipped?

options.text: Inventory of the servers
options.rationale: They knew which servers to patch.

options.text: Checking the vendor's release date
options.rationale: The date isn't a step that prevents crashes.

options.text: Documenting the change
options.rationale: Missing documentation didn't cause the crashes.

options.text: Testing before deployment
options.rationale: Correct: test before production, with a rollback plan.

questions.explanation: Patch management is an ongoing process: inventory, identify, evaluate and test, approve, deploy, verify, and document. It is a managed process, not a single update: test before production.
questions.discriminator_tested: Test before production.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes the macOS application firewall from ufw on Linux?

options.text: The macOS firewall is off by default
options.rationale: True, but not the difference in how rules work.

options.text: ufw is a separate firewall from netfilter
options.rationale: ufw is a front-end to netfilter.

options.text: macOS rules are per app; ufw's are port-based
options.rationale: Correct: per-application vs port/address rules.

options.text: macOS has no firewall; ufw is Linux-specific
options.rationale: macOS has a built-in application firewall.

questions.explanation: The macOS application firewall is off by default and sets rules per application (with pf underneath). Linux netfilter is managed via iptables/nftables or front-ends such as ufw and firewalld, using port and address rules.
questions.discriminator_tested: macOS rules per application; Linux rules port/address-based.

questions.stem: Which command gives a script's owner full access, its group read and execute, and others read alone?

options.text: chmod 745 report.sh
options.rationale: Group and others are swapped.

options.text: chmod 754 report.sh
options.rationale: Correct: 7 = rwx, 5 = r-x, 4 = r--.

options.text: chmod 457 report.sh
options.rationale: Owner would have read alone, others everything.

options.text: chown 754 report.sh
options.rationale: chown changes ownership, not permissions.

questions.explanation: Linux permissions are read (4), write (2), and execute (1) for owner, group, and others, set with chmod; the three digits are owner, group, others. chown changes ownership.
questions.discriminator_tested: Three digits = owner, group, others.

questions.stem: A NIC vendor releases a firmware fix for a remote-code-execution flaw. What is the BEST way to apply it?

options.text: Wait for Windows Update to deliver it
options.rationale: Device firmware often doesn't come through Windows Update.

options.text: Install it as soon as possible
options.rationale: Urgent, but not at the cost of skipping verification.

options.text: Vendor download, verified hash, stable power
options.rationale: Correct: right source, integrity check, and no interruption.

options.text: Use a copy from a forum mirror for speed
options.rationale: Unverified sources may be tampered with.

questions.explanation: Driver and firmware updates fix bugs and vulnerabilities in device firmware. Obtain them from the vendor and verify integrity; interrupting a firmware update can brick the device.
questions.discriminator_tested: Obtain from the vendor and verify integrity.

questions.stem: Which phase of the OS life cycle means the vendor no longer issues security patches?

options.text: Mainstream support
options.rationale: Full patching and new features.

options.text: Extended support
options.rationale: Security patches continue during extended support.

options.text: End of support
options.rationale: Correct: no further security patches.

options.text: General availability
options.rationale: That is the release.

questions.explanation: The OS life cycle runs release, mainstream support, extended support, then end of support (end of life). After end of support there are no security patches.
questions.discriminator_tested: After end of support, no security patches.

questions.stem: Which two events would an analyst find in the Windows Security log? (Choose two.)

options.text: 4625 failed logon for jlee
options.rationale: Correct: logons are audited in the Security log.

options.text: 1102 audit log cleared
options.rationale: Correct: recorded in the Security log.

options.text: A disk driver timeout
options.rationale: Drivers log to the System log.

options.text: An Excel crash report
options.rationale: Programs log to the Application log.

options.text: A router's %LINK-3-UPDOWN message
options.rationale: Routers send syslog; it isn't a Windows log.

questions.explanation: Event Viewer's Security log holds logons and audited actions, such as 4624 logon, 4625 failed logon, and 1102 log cleared. System covers OS components and drivers; Application covers programs.
questions.discriminator_tested: Security = logons and audited actions.

questions.stem: An administrator with full rights could delete a server's audit log to hide their actions. Which control BEST protects the audit trail?

options.text: Encrypt the server's disk with BitLocker
options.rationale: The admin can read and delete files on the encrypted disk.

options.text: Enable more detailed audit policy settings
options.rationale: Records more, but the admin can still delete it.

options.text: Rotate the log file more often
options.rationale: Rotation doesn't stop deletion.

options.text: Forward logs off the server
options.rationale: Correct: a copy the admin can't alter survives deletion.

questions.explanation: Audit logs record who did what, when, and from where; they are an accountability trail and must be protected from tampering, for example by sending copies to a system the admin doesn't control.
questions.discriminator_tested: Audit logs must be protected from tampering.

questions.stem: Which change BEST secures syslog traffic crossing an untrusted network?

options.text: Raise the logging level to 7
options.rationale: More messages, no more protection.

options.text: Syslog over UDP 162
options.rationale: That is the SNMP trap port, and still cleartext.

options.text: Syslog over TCP 514
options.rationale: More reliable, but still cleartext.

options.text: Syslog over TLS on TCP 6514
options.rationale: Correct: encrypted and reliable.

questions.explanation: Syslog defaults to UDP 514, which is cleartext and unreliable. TCP adds reliability; TLS (port 6514) adds security.
questions.discriminator_tested: TLS 6514 adds security.

questions.stem: Logs from 50 devices reach the syslog collector, but their timestamps disagree by several minutes, making the timeline unreliable. What is MOST likely missing?

options.text: A higher logging level on each device
options.rationale: More messages, same wrong clocks.

options.text: Syslog over TLS
options.rationale: Encryption doesn't fix timestamps.

options.text: NTP for consistent time
options.rationale: Correct: a central collector needs synchronized clocks.

options.text: A SIEM to correlate the events
options.rationale: A SIEM needs consistent time too; it can't fix bad clocks.

questions.explanation: A syslog collector is a central server receiving syslog from many devices. Its copy survives a compromised device, but building a timeline requires consistent time (NTP).
questions.discriminator_tested: A central collector requires consistent time (NTP).

questions.stem: In the message below, which part is the facility?
questions.exhibit: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface GigabitEthernet0/2, changed state to up

options.text: LINEPROTO
options.rationale: Correct: the facility comes first.
That is the severity.

options.text: UPDOWN
options.rationale: That is the mnemonic.

options.text: Gi0/2
options.rationale: That is part of the description.

questions.explanation: Cisco syslog messages use the format %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC: description. The number in the middle is the severity level.
questions.discriminator_tested: %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC.

questions.stem: A router is configured with 'logging trap 3'. Which two of these messages are sent to the syslog server? (Choose two.)

options.text: %LINK-3-UPDOWN
options.rationale: Correct: level 3 itself is included.

options.text: %SYS-6-LOGGINGHOST_STARTSTOP
options.rationale: Level 6 is informational.

options.text: %SYS-2-MALLOCFAIL
options.rationale: Correct: level 2 is more severe than 3.

options.text: %SYS-4-CONFIG_RESOLVE
options.rationale: Level 4 is less severe than 3.

options.text: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN
options.rationale: Level 5 is less severe than 3.

questions.explanation: Logging levels run 0 Emergency to 7 Debugging. A lower number is more severe, and setting level N logs N and everything more severe (0 to N).
questions.discriminator_tested: Level N logs 0 to N.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why anomaly detection in logs needs a baseline?

options.text: Baselines encrypt the logs for storage
options.rationale: Baselines describe normal activity; they don't encrypt.

options.text: Baselines reduce the number of alerts
options.rationale: Often a result, but not why one is needed.

options.text: Unusual can only be judged against normal
options.rationale: Correct: without a baseline, nothing stands out.

options.text: Baselines list known attack signatures
options.rationale: Signatures are a different detection method.

questions.explanation: Identifying anomalies means comparing log activity to a baseline: off-hours logons, repeated failures, new admin accounts, unusual traffic. An anomaly needs a baseline.
questions.discriminator_tested: Anomaly needs a baseline.

questions.stem: A security tool raises the alert below. Which capability BEST explains how it was produced?
questions.exhibit:
Rule: Brute force followed by success        Severity: High
  10:02-10:06  firewall  812 denied RDP attempts   src=198.51.100.77
  10:07        dc01      4624 logon success        user=svc-scan  src=198.51.100.77

options.text: Encrypting logs in transit to the server
options.rationale: Encryption doesn't detect anything.

options.text: Collecting logs from the firewall and server
options.rationale: Collection is needed, but linking the events made the alert.

options.text: A single device's log level being raised
options.rationale: The alert spans two devices.

options.text: Correlating events from separate sources
options.rationale: Correct: firewall and domain controller events were linked.

questions.explanation: A SIEM aggregates, normalizes, and correlates logs from many sources, raising alerts. A syslog collector stores logs; a SIEM analyzes them.
questions.discriminator_tested: SIEM correlates across sources.
